transcript.content: Hello. What brings you into the clinic today?

I'm here because people keep acting like I'm imagining it, but I know the hospital people and some folks from the agency have been watching our house and my cleaning routes to see if I'm taking proper care of my husband. It's just like when I was working at that big house out on Elm Street, you know, the one with the huge oak tree in the front yard? The lady there, Mrs. Higgins, she always thought I wasn't dusting the baseboards right, and she'd follow me around with a white glove. Can you believe that? A white glove in this day and age! Anyway, my husband likes his dinner exactly at 6:00 PM, and if I'm late because I'm trying to dodge these people watching me, he gets so cranky. He used to work at the auto plant before his back gave out. They made good cars back then, not like the plastic things they sell now. I used to have a Chevy Nova, cherry red. Loved that car. But yeah, they're definitely watching me, taking notes on how I do things.
Have you ever heard people talking or heard any sounds that others around you couldn't hear?

Well, yes, actually. Even when the house is completely quiet, I'll hear this woman's voice. It usually comes from right near the kitchen window, and it's as clear as if she were standing right next to me. She tells me to go check the locks or move my husband's pills around. Speaking of pills, he takes so many now, it's like a whole pharmacy on the counter. The little orange ones are for his blood pressure, I think. We used to go to that pharmacy on Main Street, the one with the soda fountain? Oh, they had the best cherry phosphates. You just don't see soda fountains anymore. Everything is big chain stores now, all bright lights and self-checkout machines that never work right. "Unexpected item in the bagging area," it always says. Drives me up the wall. But yes, that woman's voice, it's very clear. I always check the window, but nobody's there.
Aside from the stress of feeling watched, how has your mood been lately—have you been feeling consistently down, sad, or depressed?

Down? No, I wouldn't say I've been feeling sad. I really don't have the time to sit around feeling depressed, not with all the work I have to get done. Just yesterday I was scrubbing the grout in the master bathroom over at the Miller's house—they have this beautiful white subway tile, you know? But grout is just a complete nightmare to keep clean. I tried one of those new bleach pens they advertise on TV. Have you seen those commercials? The ones with the little animated scrubbing bubbles? I always loved those commercials when I was younger. My brother used to try and draw them on his school folders. He was such a good artist, he actually won a blue ribbon at the county fair back in, oh, it must have been '82, for a charcoal drawing of a horse. A palomino, I think it was. Beautiful animals, horses. I always wanted to ride one but my husband is terribly allergic to hay, so we never went near the stables. But anyway, no, my mood is fine, I'm not sad. Just busy trying to keep everything clean before they write it down.

Sleep? Oh, well, it's funny you ask that because lately I haven't really needed much at all. Many nights I'll just sleep maybe two or three hours, and then I'm wide awake, completely ready to go. I'll get up and start scrubbing the kitchen floors or sorting through all the old mail and papers on the dining table. I'm not even tired like I used to be when I wouldn't get a full night's rest. It's actually been great for getting things done. Speaking of getting things done, I found this huge stack of old magazines while I was sorting—National Geographics, mostly. My uncle used to collect them, he had them stacked floor to ceiling in his den. He was a bit of a hoarder, bless his heart. You could barely walk through his house without knocking over a pile of newspapers or something. He always said he was going to read them all one day, but he never did. He ended up moving to Florida, you know, for his arthritis. The humidity down there is supposed to be terrible for your hair, though. I could never live anywhere that humid, my hair would just frizz up like a poodle. But yeah, I just don't seem to need much sleep right now.

My first job was at a dry cleaner's when I was sixteen. I used to operate this massive steam press—it was terrifying at first, honestly. The steam would just billow out and the whole room smelled like starch and hot cotton. The owner, Mr. Henderson, he was missing half his left index finger. He said it was from a meat slicer accident, but my friend Sarah swore he lost it in a poker game. Sarah always had the wildest stories. She ended up moving to California to become an actress, but I think she ended up working at a car rental place near the airport. Those places always seem so stressful, people rushing around trying to catch flights. I haven't been on a plane since my honeymoon. We went to Niagara Falls. It was beautiful, but the mist ruins your shoes. What were you asking me about? I don't really keep track of my moods like that.

When my what? When I wasn't feeling so energetic? Well, actually, yes. There was a quieter spell, maybe for several weeks, where I was sleeping a lot more. I wasn't rushing around cleaning everything in sight. I was just taking it easy, which is rare for me. But even then, I still heard the voice right by the kitchen window. And I still knew the agency was watching us. It's so unnerving, having someone watch you in your own kitchen. I have these lovely sheer curtains in there, the kind with the little embroidered daisies along the hem. I bought them at a discount store two towns over. It was a Tuesday, I remember, because they have senior discount day on Tuesdays, even though I don't technically qualify yet, but the cashier just waved me through. She was chewing bubblegum, the bright pink kind that smells like strawberries. I haven't chewed gum since I got a filling on my back molar. The dentist warned me it might pull the filling right out. He had the softest hands, Dr. Miller did. Not the Miller whose house I clean, a different Miller. It's a very common name, isn't it? Like Smith or Jones. But yes, even when I was resting and sleeping more, the voice was there, and I knew they were watching.
